summary: Describes the Media Server Markup Language (MSML), an XML-based language used to control and invoke services on IP media servers. Clients can define conferencing, play and record media, and similar tasks. It is informational and was initially driven by RadiSys, with contributions from others.

eli5.summary: A media server is like a studio that can mix voices and play recordings. This is the written language you use to give the studio its instructions.

questions: how to control a media server with xml
how does msml work over sip
what is the msml core package
subtitle: An XML language that lets an application server tell a media server how to mix calls, play prompts and record audio.

tldr.problem: Media servers hold pools of conferencing and IVR resources, and applications need a standard way to reconfigure them during a call without touching the underlying SIP dialog or RTP session.
tldr.mechanism: MSML is an XML language, carried in SIP INFO or the SIP Control Framework, that creates conferences, joins and unjoins media streams, starts dialogs such as announcements and digit collection, and audits server state. It is split into a mandatory core and optional packages.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Independent Submission for information only and is not a candidate for any Internet Standard. It states that MSML has been deployed in the industry since 2003.

today: RFC 5707 is an Informational Independent Submission published in February 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

sections.title: What MSML Is For
sections.content:
Media servers contain dynamic pools of media resources. Applications, called media server clients or control agents, build services from those resources and often change them mid-call. A call might start with an IVR dialog, join a conference, move to a sidebar conference and return. None of that changes the SIP dialog or the RTP session; it only changes how media flows inside the server.

The Media Server Markup Language (MSML) is the XML language used to control that internal flow. It can create conferences, bridge sessions together, run user-interaction dialogs such as announcements and digit collection, and apply transforms such as gain control. Dialogs can also be written in VoiceXML.

MSML is transport independent. SIP is the typical transport, and this RFC defines how to carry MSML over SIP. The authors say the interface has been deployed since 2003 in conferencing, network voice services, IVR and voice or video mail.

The IESG note says the IETF disclaims any knowledge of the fitness of this RFC for any purpose, and that publication was not based on IETF review of security, congestion control or interaction with deployed protocols.
sections.eli5: A call center has a big room of phone-mixing gear. MSML is the note you pass in saying how to wire the callers together, without hanging up on anyone.

sections.title: Packages and Profiles
sections.content:
MSML is extended through packages: sets of XML schemas that add elements and attributes. The MSML Core Package is mandatory and gives structure with no features of its own. Conferencing, dialogs and auditing are built on top of it. Each package MUST define its own XML namespace, and a package schema MUST only extend MSML, never alter it.

The Dialog Core and Dialog Base packages are required for any dialog service, while the Group, Transform, Speech, Fax Detection and Fax Send/Receive packages are optional. The Audit Core Package is needed for auditing, with Conference, Connection, Dialog and Stream audit packages beneath it.

Because a device may need only part of a package, the RFC also describes profiles. A profile names a subset of a package, for example an audio announcement profile of the Dialog Base Package. Profiles are published separately from this RFC and are not registered with IANA. How a client and server learn they share the same packages is left undefined; provisioning is expected.
sections.eli5: MSML is like a toy kit with one required base plate. You snap on only the pieces you need: a conference piece, a recording piece, a fax piece.

sections.title: Carrying MSML Over SIP
sections.content:
Two transports are defined. With SIP INFO, MSML travels in INVITE and INFO requests and responses. The target of an MSML action is never inferred from the SIP dialog it arrives on; objects are always named explicitly by identifier, so one request on any dialog can affect several objects. A client may also hold a dedicated control association, a SIP dialog with no media session.

The media server sends asynchronous events back in SIP INFO on the dialog that carried the request that caused them. If that dialog is gone, the event is discarded. A dialog that ends by a <disconnect> element is reported in a SIP BYE.

With the SIP Control Framework, the client uses CONTROL messages and the server answers with responses and REPORT messages. Each MSML package gets a hierarchical Control Package name such as msml, msml-conf, msml-dialog-base or msml-audit-stream, listed in the Control-Packages header of the INVITE that creates the control channel. The conference and audit packages do not use REPORT.

MSML dialogs can also be used directly with the SIP "Prompt and Collect" and "Announcement" services of RFC 4240, with the MSML body referenced by a cid URL.
sections.eli5: MSML notes ride inside ordinary phone-call messages, like slipping instructions into an envelope that was going to the studio anyway.

sections.title: Objects and Identifiers
sections.content:
The media server is modeled as a set of objects that source, sink or modify media streams. The classes are the network connection (conn), the conference (conf) and the dialog (dialog). Operators, such as gain control, are not objects with their own identifiers; they are properties of a media stream and are created implicitly.

A network connection terminates the RTP sessions of a call and is created through SIP. A conference is one logical mix per media type with many inputs. A dialog is an automated participant such as an announcement player or a recorder, created and destroyed through MSML.

Identifiers are made of terms in the form class:instance. Connections and conferences are independent objects with one-term identifiers such as conf:abc or conn:1234. A dialog depends on one of them, so its identifier is slash-separated, for example conf:abc/dialog:recorder. With SIP third party call control, the connection instance name MUST be the local tag the media server put on the SIP dialog.

An instance name made of a single asterisk is a wildcard for all objects with the same root and class. It can only be the right-most term, so conn:* is valid but a wildcard inside a dialog root is not.
sections.eli5: Everything in the studio gets a name tag, like room:abc or room:abc/singer:one. A star on a tag means everyone in that group.

sections.title: Execution Flow and the Core Package
sections.content:
Each MSML request is processed as a single transaction. The server MUST check that the request is well-formed and valid against the schema before running anything, and MUST confirm it has the resources for the whole transaction. If it does not, it MUST return a 520 response and run nothing. Elements run sequentially in document order, and processing MUST stop on the first error. Work already done is not rolled back.

Most elements accept an optional mark attribute. The mark of the last successfully executed element is returned in an error response, so marks should be unique. Slow elements such as <dialogstart> are forked into a separate thread, so MSML does not coordinate other operations with dialog elements.

The Core Package defines four elements. <msml> is the root and carries version="1.1". <send> delivers a named event to a target. <result> reports the outcome, with a mandatory response code and optional <description>. <event> notifies the client; the core events are msml.dialog.exit, msml.conf.nomedia and msml.conf.asn.
sections.eli5: The studio reads your note top to bottom and checks it can do everything before starting. If one step fails it stops there and tells you which step it reached.

sections.title: Conferences and Media Streams
sections.content:
The Conference Core Package manages conferences with <createconference>, <modifyconference> and <destroyconference>. A conference has a mixer per media type, described by <audiomix> and <videolayout>. If none is given, the default is a single <audiomix>. The deletewhen attribute chooses automatic deletion: nomedia (the default), nocontrol or never. The term attribute decides whether remaining SIP dialogs get a BYE when the conference ends.

Audio options include <n-loudest>, which mixes only the N participants with the most audio energy, and <asn>, which reports active speakers through the msml.conf.asn event at no more than a minimum reporting interval. Video layouts use a <root> window, positioned and prioritized <region> panes, and a <selector> such as voice activated switching (vas).

Streams are managed with <join>, <modifystream>, <unjoin> and <monitor>, with <stream> children giving the media type, direction (from-id1 or to-id1) and properties such as <gain> and <clamp>. A bare <join> makes a bidirectional audio stream. When two audio streams reach a single input the server SHOULD bridge them automatically; video is never bridged automatically, and the server MUST fail such a join.

A modify request replaces the whole definition of each mixer element it includes. Anything it does not mention MUST keep its current state, and the server MUST apply all requested changes or none.
sections.eli5: You can open a room, choose whether it mixes only the loudest talkers, arrange the video windows, and move people in and out of the room while it keeps running.

sections.title: Dialogs and Media Primitives
sections.content:
Dialog packages describe automated participants built from primitives, each doing one job on a media stream. <dialogstart> starts a dialog on a connection or conference, either inline or from a src URI, with type set to application/moml+xml for MSML or application/vxml+xml for VoiceXML. Specifying both inline content and src gives error 422. <dialogend> stops a dialog and msml.dialog.exit reports the end and any results.

The mandatory Base Package provides <play> for announcements, <record>, <dtmf> or <collect> for digit collection, <dtmfgen> and <tonegen>. Play and collect, and play and record, are composites that put a <play> inside the other element. Clients SHOULD use <collect>, which is the preferred name for <dtmf>.

Dialogs have no computation or flow control, and nothing is reported unless the dialog asks with <send> or <exit>. Primitives that are not grouped run in order. The optional Group Package adds <group> for concurrent primitives that exchange events, with parallel, serial and fullduplex topologies. Primitives set shadow variables such as play.amt, which start as the string "undefined". Events are matched by longest match on dotted names.

Other optional packages cover transforms (<vad>, <gain>, <agc>, <gate>, <clamp>, <relay>), speech recognition and text to speech, fax detection, and fax send and receive.
sections.eli5: A dialog is a little robot helper in the room. It can read out a message, listen for button presses, or record what you say, and it only reports back when you tell it to.

sections.title: Auditing Server State
sections.content:
The optional Audit Core Package lets a client ask what the media server is currently doing. An <audit> request names a conference or connection in queryid (wildcards allowed) and may list states to read in statelist. State names use dot notation starting with audit. and the object class, such as audit.conf, and an asterisk wildcard may appear only as the last field.

The server MUST answer with one <auditresult> per active object in scope. Zero results means no active resources match. Child elements of each result mirror the dotted state name. Conference, Connection, Dialog and Stream audit packages define the actual state lists. The Dialog and Stream packages MUST be used with either the Conference or Connection audit package.
sections.eli5: Audit is asking the studio manager, "Who is in each room, and what are they doing right now?" and getting a tidy list back.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
The response attribute of <result> carries a numeric code. 200 means OK, 1xx is reserved, 4xx are request errors and 5xx are server errors. Some codes also appear in the namelist of a failed msml.dialog.exit event.

Request errors cover malformed XML content and attributes (401 to 410), problems with dialog languages or documents (420 to 426), object naming and existence (430 to 434) and media compatibility when joining (440 to 451). Server errors include 500 internal error, 510 not in service, 520 no resource to fulfill the request and 521 internal limit exceeded. On failure the result SHOULD describe the reason and how much of the transaction ran.
sections.eli5: Every answer comes with a number, like a score. 200 means "done", the 400s mean "your note had a mistake", and the 500s mean "the studio had a problem".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MSML is XML, so the security considerations of RFC 3023 apply. MSML interfaces are driven by a SIP application server, and clients SHOULD have an authorized security relationship with the media server, but MSML itself defines no authorization mechanism.

Where integrity or confidentiality of MSML transactions matters, the SIP control channel SHOULD use sips: and TLS. Media streams MAY be protected with SRTP, but negotiating that is initiated by clients and is outside what MSML specifies.
sections.eli5: Only trusted helpers should be allowed to give the studio orders, and secret notes should go in a locked envelope.
